questions.stem: Which experience lets an analyst build a query over warehouse tables by dragging and combining steps, without writing any T-SQL by hand?
questions.explanation: The visual query editor gives a no-code, diagram-style surface for building a query, and shows the generated T-SQL alongside it. The SQL query editor is for writing statements directly, a KQL queryset targets Eventhouse data, and a notebook is code-first.
questions.sourceSkillBullet: Select, filter, and aggregate data by using the Visual Query Editor

questions.stem: The transformation steps offered by the visual query editor will look familiar to anyone who has used which other Microsoft tool?
questions.explanation: The visual query editor uses the Power Query diagram experience, so merges, appends, groupings and column operations behave the way a Power Query user expects. That is why the same skills carry across from Dataflow Gen2 authoring.
questions.sourceSkillBullet: Select, filter, and aggregate data by using the Visual Query Editor

questions.stem: You have built a query visually and want other people to query the same shaped result from T-SQL. What is the most direct way to make that possible?
options: Save the query as a view in the warehouse
Export the result to CSV and re-import it
Copy the generated T-SQL into every consumer's query
Create a semantic model over the query
questions.answer: Save the query as a view in the warehouse
questions.explanation: Saving as a view persists the query definition in the warehouse, so anyone with permission can select from it by name and always gets the current data. Copying the T-SQL around leaves several copies to maintain, and exporting to CSV freezes the result at a point in time.
questions.sourceSkillBullet: Select, filter, and aggregate data by using the Visual Query Editor

questions.stem: In a T-SQL query that groups sales by region, which clause keeps only those regions whose total exceeds a threshold?
questions.explanation: WHERE filters rows before they are grouped, so it cannot see a group total. HAVING is evaluated after aggregation and is therefore the clause that can compare against SUM or COUNT. Getting these two the wrong way round is one of the most common T-SQL mistakes.
questions.sourceSkillBullet: Select, filter, and aggregate data by using SQL

questions.stem: An orders table has one row per order and many orders per customer. Which expression returns how many different customers placed an order?
questions.explanation: COUNT(CustomerKey) and COUNT(*) both count rows, so a customer with five orders is counted five times. DISTINCT collapses the repeats and gives the number of unique customers. SUM would add the key values together, which is meaningless.
questions.sourceSkillBullet: Select, filter, and aggregate data by using SQL

questions.stem: You need a running total of daily revenue alongside each day's own revenue, in a single result set. Which T-SQL construct gives you that?
options: A window function, SUM(Revenue) OVER (ORDER BY OrderDate)
A self-join of the table to itself on a date range
A HAVING clause comparing to a running value
questions.answer: A window function, SUM(Revenue) OVER (ORDER BY OrderDate)
questions.explanation: A window function computes an aggregate across a frame of rows while still returning every row, which is exactly what a running total needs. GROUP BY would collapse the detail away. A self-join can produce the same numbers but reads badly and performs worse, and HAVING operates on groups rather than an ordered frame.
questions.sourceSkillBullet: Select, filter, and aggregate data by using SQL

questions.stem: Which KQL operator restricts a table to the rows matching a condition?
questions.explanation: where filters rows, project chooses which columns to return, extend adds a calculated column, and summarize aggregates. Reaching for where first is also the single biggest performance habit in KQL, because it cuts the data every later operator has to touch.
questions.sourceSkillBullet: Select, filter, and aggregate data by using KQL

questions.stem: Which KQL operator produces a count of events grouped by device?
questions.explanation: summarize is the aggregation operator, and its by clause names the grouping columns, so this is KQL's equivalent of GROUP BY. project and extend shape columns rather than aggregate, and distinct returns unique combinations without counting them.
questions.sourceSkillBullet: Select, filter, and aggregate data by using KQL

questions.stem: You want one row per hour showing how many events arrived in that hour. Which KQL function rounds each timestamp down into an hourly bucket so summarize can group on it?
questions.explanation: bin rounds a value down to a multiple of the given bin size, so bin(Timestamp, 1h) turns every timestamp in an hour into the same value and summarize can group on it. It is the standard way to build a time series in KQL, and it works on numbers as well as datetimes.
questions.sourceSkillBullet: Select, filter, and aggregate data by using KQL

questions.stem: Which DAX function removes the filters currently applied to a table, so a measure can report a total that ignores a slicer?
questions.explanation: REMOVEFILTERS clears filters from the specified table or columns, which is how a measure reports an unfiltered total. KEEPFILTERS does the opposite by preserving existing filters, FILTER adds one, and RELATED follows a relationship to fetch a value.
questions.sourceSkillBullet: Select, filter, and aggregate data by using DAX

questions.stem: Line total must be quantity multiplied by unit price, computed for each row and then added up, without adding a calculated column. Which DAX expression does that?
questions.explanation: SUMX is an iterator: it evaluates the expression once per row and then sums the results, which is what a row-by-row product requires. SUM takes a single column and cannot accept an expression. Multiplying the two totals together is a different and wrong number, since it multiplies every quantity by every price in aggregate.
questions.sourceSkillBullet: Select, filter, and aggregate data by using DAX

questions.stem: A measure must show each product's sales as a share of sales across all products, while a product slicer is active. Which denominator is correct?
questions.explanation: The denominator has to escape the product filter, and CALCULATE with REMOVEFILTERS on the Product table does exactly that. A plain SUM inherits the current filter and would give each product a share of itself, which is always 100 percent.
questions.sourceSkillBullet: Select, filter, and aggregate data by using DAX
